led.name: LED
led.what: An LED is a tiny light. It glows when electricity flows through it the right way.
led.legs: The long leg is + (the anode). The short leg is − (the cathode), on the side where the rim is flat.
led.did_you_know: LED stands for light-emitting diode. LEDs use far less power than old light globes and can last for 50,000 hours.

rgb-led.name: RGB LED
rgb-led.what: An RGB LED is three tiny lights in one: red, green and blue. Mix them to make almost any colour.
rgb-led.legs: The longest leg is − (common cathode). The single leg beside it is red, and on the other side are green, then blue.
rgb-led.did_you_know: Your screen makes every colour you see with tiny red, green and blue dots, just like this LED.

resistor-220.name: 220Ω resistor
resistor-220.what: A resistor slows down the electricity. A 220Ω resistor keeps an LED from getting too much and burning out.
resistor-220.legs: It works either way round. Read its colour bands: red, red, brown means 220Ω.
resistor-220.did_you_know: The coloured bands are a code. Red is 2 and brown means 'add one zero', so red-red-brown is 22 then 0: 220.

resistor-10k.name: 10kΩ resistor
resistor-10k.what: A 10kΩ resistor slows electricity a lot. Two of them can share a voltage, like turning 5V into 2.5V.
resistor-10k.legs: It works either way round. Read its colour bands: brown, black, orange means 10,000Ω (10kΩ).
resistor-10k.did_you_know: The k in 10k means 'thousand', just like in kilometre. So 10kΩ is 10,000 ohms.

button.name: push button
button.what: A push button joins two wires while you press it. Your code can check if it's pressed.
button.legs: It has four legs. The two legs on each side are always joined. Pressing the button joins the left side to the right side.
button.did_you_know: Computer keyboards have a tiny button like this under every key.

buzzer.name: piezo buzzer
buzzer.what: A piezo buzzer makes beeps and notes. Your code chooses how high or low the note is.
buzzer.legs: The + leg is longer, or has a red wire, or a + mark on top. The other leg goes to GND.
buzzer.did_you_know: Inside is a thin crystal disc that bends when electricity flows. It bends thousands of times a second to make sound.

potentiometer.name: potentiometer
potentiometer.what: A potentiometer (pot) is a knob. Turning it changes a number your board can read, from 0 up to the top.
potentiometer.legs: The middle leg is the wiper: it goes to an analog pin. The two outside legs go to power and GND.
potentiometer.did_you_know: Old radios used potentiometers for the volume knob. Many guitar amps still do!

joystick.name: joystick
joystick.what: A joystick is two knobs in one: left–right and up–down. You can also press it down like a button.
joystick.legs: The pins are labelled: GND, +5V (power), VRx (left–right), VRy (up–down) and SW (the press).
joystick.did_you_know: Game controllers have joysticks just like this one inside their thumbsticks.

keypad-4x4.name: 4×4 keypad
keypad-4x4.what: A keypad has 16 buttons in rows and columns. Your code works out which key you pressed.
keypad-4x4.legs: It has eight pins on its ribbon: four rows (R1 to R4) then four columns (C1 to C4), from left to right.
keypad-4x4.did_you_know: With rows and columns, 16 keys need only 8 wires. A big keyboard uses the same trick.

servo.name: servo motor
servo.what: A servo is a motor that turns to the angle you choose, from 0° to 180°, and holds there.
servo.legs: It has three wires: brown (or black) is GND, red is power (5V) and orange (or yellow) is the signal.
servo.did_you_know: Servos steer remote-control cars and move the arms of robots.

ldr.name: light sensor (LDR)
ldr.what: A light sensor (LDR) lets more electricity through in bright light. Your board reads it as a number.
ldr.legs: It works either way round. It's used with a 10kΩ resistor so the board can measure the light.
ldr.did_you_know: LDR stands for light-dependent resistor. Street lights use sensors like this to turn on at night.

hc-sr04.name: ultrasonic distance sensor (HC-SR04)
hc-sr04.what: An ultrasonic sensor measures distance. It squeaks too high for us to hear and times the echo, like a bat.
hc-sr04.legs: The pins are labelled: VCC (5V), Trig, Echo and Gnd. On a 3.3V board, Echo needs two resistors to make it safe.
hc-sr04.did_you_know: Sound travels about 343 metres every second, so an echo from 1 metre away comes back in under a hundredth of a second.

pir.name: motion sensor (PIR)
pir.what: A motion sensor (PIR) notices warm things moving, like people. It sends a signal when it sees movement.
pir.legs: It has three pins: VCC (power), OUT (the signal) and GND. Some boards label them on the back under the white dome.
pir.did_you_know: PIR stands for passive infrared. It sees the heat your body gives off, even in the dark.

dht.name: temperature and humidity sensor (DHT11 / DHT22)
dht.what: A DHT sensor measures temperature and humidity (how damp the air is).
dht.legs: The module has three pins: S (data), + (power) and − (GND).
dht.did_you_know: Weather stations measure humidity because damp air makes hot days feel even hotter.

soil-moisture.name: soil moisture sensor
soil-moisture.what: A soil moisture sensor tells you how wet the soil is, so you know when a plant needs water.
soil-moisture.legs: It has three pins: VCC (power), GND and SIG (the signal, to an analog pin). The two long prongs go in the soil.
soil-moisture.did_you_know: Wet soil lets electricity flow more easily than dry soil. That's how the sensor knows!

rfid-rc522.name: RFID reader (RC522) and cards
rfid-rc522.what: An RFID reader can read cards and tags without touching them. Each card has its own number.
rfid-rc522.legs: Its 8 pins are labelled. It needs 3.3V, never 5V. SDA, SCK, MOSI and MISO talk to the board, RST resets it and IRQ isn't used.
rfid-rc522.did_you_know: Bus cards, library cards and school passes often use RFID.

oled.name: OLED screen (SSD1306)
oled.what: An OLED screen is a tiny screen (128 × 64 dots) that can show words, numbers and pictures.
oled.legs: It has four pins: GND, VCC (power), SCL and SDA. SCL and SDA go to the board's I2C pins.
oled.did_you_know: Each dot on an OLED makes its own light, so black parts of the picture use no power at all.

lcd-i2c.name: 16×2 LCD screen (I2C)
lcd-i2c.what: An LCD screen shows two lines of 16 letters. The little board on the back means it needs only four wires.
lcd-i2c.legs: The four pins on the back are GND, VCC (5V), SDA and SCL. SDA and SCL go to the board's I2C pins.
lcd-i2c.did_you_know: Each letter is drawn with a grid of 5 × 8 dots. Look closely and you'll see them!

tm1637.name: 4-digit display (TM1637)
tm1637.what: A 4-digit display shows numbers, like a digital clock, with a colon in the middle.
tm1637.legs: It has four pins: CLK, DIO, VCC (power) and GND.
tm1637.did_you_know: Each digit has 7 bars (segments). Lighting different bars makes the numbers 0 to 9.

led-matrix.name: 8×8 LED matrix (MAX7219)
led-matrix.what: An LED matrix is a grid of 64 red LEDs (8 × 8). You can light any of them to draw pictures and games.
led-matrix.legs: Use the five pins at the DIN end: VCC, GND, DIN, CS and CLK. The pins at the other end can join another matrix.
led-matrix.did_you_know: The MAX7219 chip on the back controls all 64 LEDs, so your board needs only three wires to talk to it.

neopixel-ring.name: NeoPixel ring (WS2812)
neopixel-ring.what: A NeoPixel ring is a circle of 12 colour LEDs. Your code can set every one to its own colour.
neopixel-ring.legs: Use the pins marked PWR (5V), GND and Data Input (DI). Data Out joins another ring.
neopixel-ring.did_you_know: Every NeoPixel has its own tiny chip inside, so one wire can control hundreds of them.

neopixel-strip.name: NeoPixel strip (WS2812)
neopixel-strip.what: A NeoPixel strip is a line of 8 colour LEDs. Your code can set every one to its own colour.
neopixel-strip.legs: Use the pins at the DIN end: 4-7VDC (power), DIN (data in) and GND. The other end joins another strip.
neopixel-strip.did_you_know: Light shows at concerts often use long strips of LEDs like these.
